key_insight: Droplet impact loads on wind turbine blades can be predicted from a universal scaling law based on droplet projection area, even for non-spherical shapes and non-normal impacts.
engineering_relevance: This gives blade designers and maintenance planners a more realistic way to estimate leading-edge erosion risk from rain and sea spray than idealized spherical-droplet models.
method: Built a fluid-structure interaction framework coupling incompressible multiphase flow with finite element blade-material analysis.
Simulated droplet impacts with arbitrary shapes and orientations instead of ideal spherical, normal-incidence cases.
Derived a scaling law linking peak pressure, peak force, and peak-force timing to droplet projection area.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent correlations across simulations: larger projection area increases peak pressure, influential area, and peak force, while time to peak force decreases as expected from momentum conservation.
watch_item: The scaling law should be validated against experiments and real atmospheric droplet populations before being used for certification or life prediction.
paper_title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades
